maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Can the Prime Minister
tell us who represented Canada last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
At the last
assembly we had three delegates, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and Senator Dandurand. The delegation also included Doctor Skelton, Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs; Mr. Vanier, who is in the London office, and Doctor Riddell.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the question put by the hon. gentleman who spoke immediately preceding the Prime Minister provokes me to make one or two observations in connection with the personnel of the Canadian delegation that attended the last assembly of the league.
I have criticized a good many of those who represented Canada at the League of Nations, and I know it was not because of anything that I had said, but perhaps in spite of it, that the delegation this year was of an exceptionally high order. I had the privilege of attending on my own account the last assembly of the league and of being present at its discussions both in committee and in general assembly, and I am sure I am expressing an opinion that will be shared by every member of the house when I say that we must always feel it a great honour for Canada to have been represented at the league by the Prime Minister and the ministers and others in attendance with him.
I seem to have been in the habit of following prime ministers. I was in Geneva when Sir Robert Borden was in attendance, and I was also at Geneva when the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was likewise head of the Canadian delegation. I want to say first of all about his representation that unfortunately bis indisposition at the moment precluded him from giving that attention which normally he would have given to the affairs of the league, but his was a representation of a very high character. The Prime Minister of Canada when he attends the assembly of the League of Nations gives to the delegation a distinction and a prestige which normally it does not possess, and that was particularly true, Mr. Chairman, this year. I think some mention should be made of the character of that delegation.
There was first of all the Prime Minister. I have taken pains to go through the list of all the delegates, and our Prime Minister was the only head of a government in attendance

at this year's assembly. In addition we were represented by two other ministers of the crown, the Minister of Labour and Senator Dandurand; also by Doctor Skelton and Colonel Vanier. Of equal importance is the fact, which should be noted by the committee and which has not been mentioned for obvious reasons, that the Prime Minister of Canada was singled out for very high distinction at the assembly, having been selected as one of the four vice-presidents.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that members of the house on all sides are fully convinced of the importance of proper representation at international conferences generally, and it is a source of gratification to the country that the government decided to send a delegation so fully representative of Canadian thought, and clothed with the fullest authority.
While I am on my feet may I make one or two other observations that are made from a study over a period of some time. I believe we are fast approaching the period when we should have in this country a foreign service act. That may not be altogether in harmony with the views of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I believe it is essential that not only those in charge of our legations but as well those who are acting in minor capacities in our legations should be given ample opportunity, particularly if their own pecuniary circumstances do not permit, to keep fully in touch with what is going on in this country. I know at least two gentlemen in our foreign service who have not visited Canada for some time, who have not had the means to come to Canada. One in particular, in my judgment, in spite of his good intentions and wishes, is no longer seized with the current thought of his own country. I think that is to be deplored. It should be possible for minor and major officials to visit their own country periodically, as officials of the League of Nations are permitted to do, and indeed as minor officials in other legations of other countries are permitted to do.
I simply make these observations, Mr. Chairman, but I think they have great merit. In conclusion, it does seem to me that the time has come in this house when these matters- I do not refer particularly to the Geneva estimates but rather to questions coming within the category of international affairs- should be discussed by a properly constituted committee. If we are to attain some measure of thoroughness in dealing with them we should pursue in respect of international affairs the same course that we pursue in respect of our purely domestic problems.

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Might I venture to agree with and if necessary supplement what has just been said by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). It does seem to me that there ought to be a better opportunity given to the house to study our foreign affairs than is given upon consideration of the estimates. We have a committee known as the industrial and international relations committee. It is only occasionally that any matter referring to international relations has been referred to that committee, and I am afraid the committee has not been taken very seriously. The whole range of matters coming under external affairs, at least those that are not strictly confidential in character, might automatically be referred to that committee. The members of the committee would benefit very largely by their study. Certain representations by the committee might be made to the house. It could have before it the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, who might at least outline many of the problems that face us at this time. There should be before the committee a detailed report of what was done at the last assembly of the League of Nations. Only as members of the house secure fuller knowledge of international affairs than most of us have at the present time can it be hoped that there will be a deep interest in these matters on the part of the people generally. On several occasions I have spoken to the Prime Minister about this matter. I hope he will see his way clear in the near future either to refer these matters to the present committee or, even better, to appoint a separate committee charged with studying on behalf of the house the whole of our foreign policy and international relations generally, as is done-a colleague suggests-by the foreign relations committee in the United States.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I have followed from time to time the statements made by members of this house who suggested that the foreign policy of Canada should be studied by a committee, and the more I have looked into the matter the more certain I am that it would do harm rather than good. No one would suggest that the foreign relations committee at Washington has at all times served a useful purpose. The essence of foreign policy in England, for instance, has been continuity of policy and, so far as might be, unity of thought and action on the part of successive governments; that is a Liberal government succeeding a Conservative administration has endeavoured to carry out the general outline of large policy which its predecessors thought desirable in the interests of the country. Public
examination into details of foreign relations tends to create the impression that that which must be withheld from the public has a sinister meaning, though in fact it has not. One cannot discuss foreign problems-and when I use the word "foreign" I employ it in the sense of everything external to Canada-as one discusses domestic problems, because the other man's point of view must be considered, and yet it cannot be disclosed; he does not do business on that assumption, and without his specific consent his communications or dispatches or expressions of viewpoint cannot be made known to the public.
One of the difficulties in connection with foreign policy that have been experienced by countries which have pursued the course that has just been suggested is that they find it hard to do business in the way in which foreign relations have usually been maintained. The essence of democratic government is that so far as possible the government shall be responsive to the mind and will of the people. But if people's minds are to be distracted by extreme views and the suggestion of sinister purposes and motives in connection with matters that cannot be fully exposed at the moment to the public mind, because their disclosure must be delayed until something further has occurred, a government may experience the negation of the very effort it is making to secure a successful issue of the matter in which it is engaged. During the last few months every government in the civilized world has been worried and worn by the conditions that obtain throughout the world. Now if we are to resolve ourselves into a committee, small or large, and have statements made by prominent officials, and examine documents and papers, when an announcement is made that this or that paper cannot be produced at the moment, someone will say, "Why can we not have it? Are we not the people?" and the net result will be that you will create an atmosphere unfavourable to the sense of tranquillity and confidence on the part of the public which every government, I think, aims to secure.
When Lord Granville went out of office in 1870 he told his successor that the horizon had never been clearer than at that moment, yet within a few weeks the Franco-Prussian war broke out. That is an illustration of the uncertainties that pervade the atmosphere of foreign offices. At the moment we have no such terrific responsibilities, but our partnership in the commonwealth of nations does place us in a position wherein a public discussion by a committee of matters that I could name, were I so disposed, might and I

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
think would be most injurious in respect of many problems that are constantly engaging the attention of the prime minister and his government. For these reasons I have never been able to bring myself to an appreciation of what is meant by the proposal to refer to a committee matters relating to our foreign policy.
The foreign policy of this country is so obvious that it does not require much discussion. On points where there may be differences or wherein an acute situation may arise, the responsible ministers are always desirious of informing the public, not only for their own safety but because they have a sense of responsibility in that regard. But there are some matters which can be peacefully adjusted by reason of the very fact that they are not made known for public discussion, whereas such a result would be made difficult if they became the subject matter of bickering and unpleasant and unhappy reflections. I am certain of that. I have made it my business to ask in many quarters, not only in our own empire but elsewhere, and I have received but one answer, and it is this: with the tremendous responsibility that rests upon those who have to accept the duties of office, to meet a committee of parliament and be asked about matters which cannot be divulged because they may be in a state of partial completion, would be impossible without creating that very suspicion and unrest and distrust which all governments endeavour to prevent or allay. I cannot bring myself to any other view. I should like to feel that there was something in the suggestion that has been made, but I cannot see that it would have any effect other than to injure rather than advance the cause which the hon. member has in mind.
The discussions in the foreign relations committee of the United States are of two kinds, one public and the other private. The senate of the United States goes into executive session about every matter that affects the interests of the United States with respect to treaties when they are up for discussion and ratification, and it does not permit the general public to have any knowledge of them. It was asserted that this had always been a matter of tradition. There is said to have been such tremendous applause that the windows of the old senate chamber rattled when, in connection with the Alabama claims, Sumner quoted:
It was that fatal and perfidious bark,
Built in th' eclipse, and rigged with curses dark,
That sunk so low that sacred head of thine.

That is what he is alleged to have said at the height of his eloquence. In the United States they do not permit public discussion of those matters which are of tremendous and vital force in connection with their foreign policies. Surely there has been in this house no limitation by any government to the fullest possible discussion of every matter that affects the relations of Canada to the empire and to foreign countries; I have seen no such effort on the part of anyone, and I know of none on the part of the late government at least. But to send matters of that kind to a committee for discussion I cannot but think would have the effect of destroying that very sentiment and sense of solidarity and continuity which is so desirable in connection with our international relations, whether with other members of the British commonwealth or what one might technically call foreign nations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I might say to my hon. friend, the member for Winnipeg North Centre, that in bringing on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs at this early stage of the session, I had hoped that this year at least the government would be meeting his wishes in the matter of affording early opportunity for the fullest discussion of external affairs. Two or three times my hon. friend has complained that the estimates of the Department of External Affairs were held until near the end of the session with the result that no opportunity had been given for discussion of External Affairs. This year I tried to bring on the estimates early so as to avoid that criticism. As to ample opportunity of discussion may I say that opportunity is being offered now. The house is in committee, there is no desire in any way to limit discussion. I must say however that I agree with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has just said about the great responsibility which rests upon a minister in charge of foreign affairs to-day. If there is any time or occasion where the doctrine of ministerial responsibility applies to the full it is in these matters which relate to the affairs of foreign nations and other countries. For example, I cannot imagine a committee calling before it the under secretary for External Affairs and expecting him to take responsibility either for giving or withholding information in relation to foreign affairs. That is something for which the minister himself must take responsibility. That being the case, it seems to me it is much better that the minister should take his stand before the house as a whole rather than appear before

Supply-External Affairs-Miscellaneous
any committee. With the condition of the world what it is to-day, I feel very strongly that there are some things which it is just as well to avoid discussing. On the floor of the house a minister can give his reasons for withholding discussion and will be expected to do so. I do not see what could be added in committee that could not be given on the floor of the house.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I appreciate the kindness of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in bringing down the estimates at an early stage of the session. But it seems to me that both he and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) have a wrong idea of what is involved in my proposal. I recognize that there are certain matters which, by their very nature, must be more or less confidential. No one wants to drag those out, especially when delicate negotiations are going on. I recognize also that no under secretary ought to be asked to give information with regard to matters of policy. But I believe there is much taking place in the world to-day that ought to be known to our general public. Comparatively little information is given in our press concerning international affairs; even in our schools and universities little opportunity is given to follow them. If even we in this house are to form an intelligent judgment on these matters, an opportunity ought to be afforded for studying them.
What I speak of is the setting up of a new piece of machinery. With regard to the business of almost every department we have committees; every hon. member is familiar with what is done in those committees; the head of the department or other officials may be called in, not to discuss policy but rather to give information. Sometimes outsiders may be called in; representative men or women from many walks of life appear and give information or their expert knowledge. It is for the government to decide later what the government's policy shall be, but at least the committee is more or less informed as to the subject matter under discussion. Surely we should get away from this idea that foreign policy must be conducted in secret. The suggestion is made that if the public knows just a little more, it will become restless. I cannot see the force of that argument. The fact is that if it is considered that foreign affairs must be conducted in secrecy, the public is much more likely to imagine that something is wrong.
The leader of the opposition suggests that we ought to have continuity in our policies as regards both commonwealth affairs and dealings with foreign nations. I would suggest to
him that it did not look as if he were very strong on continuity when immediately on accession to office he altered our representation in both London and Washington.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: There was not any representation at Washington at the time.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Well, very shortly afterwards there was representation of a very different kind. I am not urging that in committee we should cover the whole field, but instead of merely passing an item to cover the expenses of our delegation to Geneva, we might well have that delegation appear before a committee, tell its experiences in Geneva, share with us some of the information acquired there. Then, with regard to relationships that we have with other countries, instead of our being forced to discuss in the house details with regard to our relations with China, Japan or any other country, it seems to me it would be far more intelligent to have some definite machinery through which this could be done to greater advantage. That is all I have in view. I do not think the answer of either the leader of the opposition or the Prime Minister has really touched the proposal which I made in this connection.

speechtext: May I ask when the vote pertaining to the International Joint Commission comes up.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: And does the International- Joint Commission report directly to the minister on matters that came up at the meetings of the commission last fall?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: The commission makes a report to the minister, yes, upon the different matters that come up for discussion.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: At the moment I have nothing to say with regard to what was discussed- at the meetings of the commission that I attended, I refer particularly to the part of the reference to the commission concerning the Richelieu river. This matter will come up under the public works department, and I shall have something to say then. I must say, however, that I was amazed at the proposal- of the Lake Champlain Valley Council Association before the commission, to divert water from lake St. Francis across country, having it flow by gravity into the Hudson river. The water level of lake St. Francis, above sea level, was proposed as stationary at 152 feet. The proposal was to run a canal directly across to lake Champlain, the water to enter that lake through one or two locks having a total drop of about fifty feet. It was proposed that the level of lake Champlain should be maintained at 100 feet above sea level by constructing works at the outlet of the lake in order to regulate the flow into the Richelieu river at, I suppose, approximately a thousand second feet. The balance of the proposed diversion of 5,000 second feet-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt, but we are on item 210, to provide for hospitality in connection with visitors.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The Prime Minister gave me permission to ask a question about an item that was not called, and in any case I shall be through in a moment. As I said, the proposal was to control the flow of water at the outlet of lake Champlain so as to maintain the level at 100 feet above sea level. Then it was proposed to tunnel or excavate through the height of land south of lake Champlain andi take the water across country to Northumberland on the Hudson river. That height of land is about 147 feet above sea level. I covered that territory very thoroughly during the fall, and I am familiar with the whole layout of the country.
It struck me, Mr. Chairman, that if anything of this sort was ever permitted it would be ruinous to the harbour of Montreal, and anything that would ruin the harbour of Montreal would ruin the whole economic fabric of this country. I am confident that the minister would never permit the diversion

of 5,000 seeond feet of water out of lake St. Francis, across country and through two locks into the Hudson river at Northumberland but if an association carries on propaganda and keeps it up for a long time there is no telling how far it may go. I wondered whether that report had been received by the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: I understand that the inquiry was originated at the instance of the United States. Some hearings have been held already, and the commission will be holding further hearings in April. It will be some time before any report is made, and when that report is prepared it will be printed and sent to the governments of both countries. The commission will not be in a position to commit either country to any project. The purpose of the inquiry is to get information which will enable the government to decide what may be best with respect to any project of the kind.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister explain this item and give us a statement as to the money expended last year?

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Just before that point is left, I wonder whether the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has given any thought to the effect of the privy council decisions, which I have read in the newspapers but of which I have not seen the full text, with regard to the meaning of section 132 in relation to the treaty having to do with the International Joint Commission. If the newspaper reports are accurate, I am not quite clear as to whether or not the treaty is invalid. Perhaps when the minister gets the opportunity, he will look into that question when he is looking into the other matters that have to be dealt with.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
My hon. friend has asked for an- explanation of the hospitality vote, which shows an increase of $10,000. This again brings up a point, which will come up in connection with -other items which will be presented this afternoon, as to the position which a country is obliged to take as a country when belonging to the family of nations. The custom does exist among different nations of extending something in the way of hospitality to important personages irom other countries. When Canada is

Supply-External Affairs-Miscellaneous
represented) abroad by its public men they are frequently entertained by the governments of the countries to which they go, and on our part we are obliged to extend similar courtesies, or at least we feel that we should do so, to distinguished personages visiting Canada from other countries. This year, due to the coronation and the imperial conference, we expect that there will be a considerable number of persons of importance visiting Canada to whom some hospitality should be extended by the government, and for that reason the amount is somewhat larger than otherwise would be the case.
I might mention in particular that we have learned that Prince Chichibu the brother of the Emperor of Japan proposes to go to London for the coronation via Canada. His Royal Highness will be visiting Ottawa on his way to London, and will be staying in this country for a short time. The government feel that it would wish to extend appropriate oourtesies to the emperor's brother.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I think there is no overestimating the importance of having this dominion properly discharge its duties to those from other parts of the British Empire and elsewhere who visit us. It will be within the memory of this house that we did entertain the brother of the Emperor of Japan and his wife, and we did1 entertain the King of Siam. They intimated that they were passing through this country, and we considered it our duty to extend some courtesy by way of entertainment. I can not in any sense come within the qualification imposed by the first minister in his observations, as being a distinguished person, but I was embarrassed by the kindness and courtesy extended to me in New Zealand, Australia and South Africa. The governments of those countries certainly make it their business to extend hospitality to people from other parts of the dominions. We have done less of this than most of our sister dominions, and in view of the great stretch of country we have it is highly important that we should provide that those who come among us and, .to put it on a selfish basis, who may do us a great deal of good, should get the best possible view of the country as they pass through it and .the best possible impression with respect to it. I feel quite certain that this view, which is held in other countries, should prevail here. As far as my information goes, there is no country that does not maintain a hospitality fluid of substantial proportions. In Canada the *accounts are audited by the auditor general, and I think it may be said in the main that there has been little cause for complaint either as to the method of inspection or as to the persons who have been selected to be what
one of our friends once described as the victims of our hospitality, there being some danger that hospitality may be extended too generously.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
A sharp issue is raised
here, in connection with advertising. It will be recalled that the former high commissioner endeavoured to consolidate in Great Britain the advertising done by Canada. The Prime Minister will recall that he directed attention to certain efforts made by one department to carry on advertising "on its own," so to speak.
The statute dealing with the office of high commissioner provides that he shall have general supervision and control of our activities in the United Kingdom. I read and always have read the statute as indicating that he should be in charge, and I use the expression "in charge" in the colloquial sense in which we use it in Canada. The former high 
commissioner endeavoured to consolidate advertising services. I believe the Prime Minister will recall that in one year we increased the vote to, I believe, about $250,000. That represented all the advertising expenditure to be made in the United Kingdom and Europe in that year, and we endeavoured to bring it under the control of the high commissioner.
Mr. James Spence, to whom reference has been made, is in charge of that section of the advertising carried on under the direction of the high commissioner's office. Various departments have endeavoured to conduct their own advertising campaigns. At one time it was the Department of Trade and Commerce, to which exception was taken, and at another time it was the Department of Agriculture. The question as to the relationship between these two departments I purpose discussing at a later time. The story is a very old one, and involves a close and careful analysis of the situation. If the Department of Trade and Commerce is to be treated as it has been on several occasions in the past, then it will fail in the discharge of its duty. That department is responsible for the trade commissioners.	.
I read an article in one of the weeklies-* I believe it was Canada's Weekly-dealing with the impingement by one department upon the operations of others. Our trade commissioners are highly efficient and effective men. The principle underlying the agricultural activities of Canada will be found in the British North America Act, and in the statute dealing with the department. It was never intended that it should be charged with a responsibility outside Canada. Its duty was to see that our products were standardized, that they were of the highest possible quality and that every possible step was taken to ensure that they met the requirements indicated by the Department of Trade and Commerce. So the trade commissioners are responsible for the work outside Canada. If the testimony to their effectiveness and efficiency that one receives in other parts of the world is correct, these men, who are mostly young, have discharged their duties and responsibilities in a highly satisfactory manner. If another body is to be set up to do the same work or to have any responsibility in connection with it, the result will be disastrous. I know that in times past acute differences have arisen between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. Those of us who have listened to the statements of a former minister of agriculture and of a former minister of trade and commerce will realize the necessity of there being a clear delimitation of their activities as provided by the statute. The

Sup-ply-External Affairs-Miscellaneous
Department of Agriculture should be charged with the responsibility of seeing that the requisitions as to fitness and quality and everything connected with the preparation of our exports have been complied with. When they leave these shores the responsibility should belong to the other department. I mention this because it touches the question of advertising. The Prime Minister says that the question of advertising does not touch the Department of Agriculture, that the statute makes it perfectly clear that the trade commissioner's office should be responsible for it all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: As my right hon. friend says, any advertising is carried on through the high commissioner. I was answering the hon. member who spoke a moment ago with reference to using money voted to the Department of Agriculture for its work. That money is used for the purpose of gathering information through officers of the department in England as to what would be helpful in determining types of commodities required and in connection with grading and the like. I think that is what my right hon. friend is referring to.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL

Item agreed to.
Expenses in connection with the negotiation of treaties, $20,000.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I trust the chairman will allow me to ask a question as to the matter which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) mentioned a moment ago. I understood him

to say that he had received copies of the judgments on the recent references which were made and came before the judicial committee of the privy council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I wonder whether it would not be possible to have them printed so that the members of the house might have access to them. It will be one or two months before the law reports are published. We have now on the order paper certain bills introduced, strange to say, by a private member for the repeal of certain statutes enacted by this parliament in 1935, and the question of their repeal must depend very largely upon a careful consideration of the opinions delivered by the judicial committee of the privy council. On that ground alone it seems to me that we should have at an early day copies of the judgments made available to all members who are interested.
Another more important matter was mentioned by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) a moment ago, and that is that the opinions of the judicial committee of the privy council, as summarized and reported in the press, seem to go to the very root of the previous constitutional practice and to suggest that the government of Canada no longer has the legal authority or the constitutional right to negotiate with foreign nations treaties except those to which the parliament of Canada can give legislative validity. As that question must, I think, come up for discussion, it is important that the text of the opinions delivered by the judicial committee of the privy council should be made available. Certainly I trust that the government will not allow certain bills which have passed a first reading to come up for a second reading until we have the text of those opinions available.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: I realize the importance of those decisions being made available to all the members of the house, and it was my intention to lay on the table to-morrow, at the first opportunity, copies of all the decisions. Then, perhaps, either the house will order that they be printed and distributed, or possibly if they are not too lengthy they might be inserted in the Votes and Proceedings, so that they would reach all the members of the house the following day.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL

And a few extra copies of the Votes and Proceedings might be printed.

Yes. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has said that certain bills for the repeal of certain legislation have already received their first reading. Those bills are still on the order paper for first reading. The decisions of the privy council doubtless have much to do with the consideration which members will give to those bills when they come up, if they do come up.
As far as the right of Canada to enter into treaties is concerned, the only references in which the question of treaties arose were the labour references respecting minimum wages, hours of labour and the weekly day of rest. They were special. It was even represented in this house that they were not treaties at all. They were conventions which were accepted by the house in 1935, and I believe it will be seem from the decisions of the privy council that their lordships did not consider them as ordinary treaties, such as my hon. friend suggests. However, we had better wait until we see the text, which I myself have not yet seen.

To provide for expenses connected with Canada's representation at the coronation of His Majesty, $35,000.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister indicate how much money altogether it is proposed to spend on the coronation ceremonies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: We have estimated $35,000 as the amount required, but that is exclusive of the $197,000 which will be required for the contingent.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, here again I am afraid I must protest against these large amounts. It seems to me that this country might very well be represented by the Prime Minister and several individuals who could represent it with dignity, but I cannot quite see why there should be these very heavy expenses for what is, after all, simply an elaborate ceremonial, I turn over to the next page of the estimates, opposite
vote 249 for $197,000 for the expenses of the contingent, and I find these grants: grant to the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare, $13,100; grant to the Canadian National1 Committee for Mental Hygiene, $10,000; grant to the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, $5,000; grant to the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, $18,000; grant to the Canadian Tuberculosis Association, $20,250; grant to the Victorian Order of Nurses, $13,100; grant to assist the Canadian branch of the St. John Ambulance Association, $4,050; grant to the Canadian Red Cross Society, $8,100; grant to the Canadian Dental Hygiene Council, $750. I give those as examples of the comparatively small grants that we make to these important institutions.
I am thinking more particularly of the large number of people who are living on very low standards, some of them in actual destitution, and who will have to pay the large sums required to send this contingent and the various delegates to London. We have just passed large votes for the advertising abroad of wheat, fish and so on, but the actual agricultural workers, the fishermen, the miners and the textile workers, whom we were discussing here last "night, and generally the great masses of the producers of this country who really are the foundation of our national life, are to-day receiving in their personal incomes very small amounts indeed. Some of them are trying to bring up families on the small wages they are receiving. I do think-though I may be the only one in the house who ventures to express himself along these lines-that we are getting away from the earlier ideals which inspired the people^ of Canada, ideals of simplicity, ideals of liv

ing within our means. We have a sort of false front; we have to live in as good a house on the international street as anybody else. This is all wrong. We are not living within our means, and in our efforts to advertise this country or to be present at a great ceremonial, we are making large expenditures, when as a matter of fact we refuse to make even comparatively small expenditures to meet the needs of the producers and of the large numbers of unemployed who are constantly begging us for alms.
. Mr. MACKENZIE KING: My hon. friend is hardly fair in the comparison he has made. He was trying to draw a contrast between what is being spent for the purpose of representation at the coronation and what is being spent in the way of money for social services. For any such purpose he ought to give the committee a statement in full, which would include what is being spent by the provinces for all social services-

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: And the municipalities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: -and what is being paid out by municipalities. He ought to take account of what has been disbursed by the federal government in the last few years in unemployment relief-

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: And by private benevolence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
-and for old age pensions, and now we have pensions for the blind which are being proposed this session. All that the hon. member has quoted are a few contributions being made from the federal treasury to help some private agencies which are carrying on a very creditable work and wish to be assured, through assistance given them by this government, of an amount sufficient to pay their secretarial staffs. I mention that only because I think it is important that a true perspective should be preserved.
With regard to the matter of representation, I believe citizens of Canada generally will wish this country to be represented at the coronation on a par with Australia and South Africa and New Zealand and India and other parts of the British empire. After all Canada is the largest and the oldest of the dominions. We take a certain pride in having a status of our own as an autonomous nation with all the powers and rights of a full nation. If we are to be represented at all at the coronation, surely it should be with some regard to the position that Canada holds in the eyes of other parts of the empire and other countries of the world.
My hon. friend speaks continually about what we are spending for one purpose and another and asks why we cannot afford a little more for peace policies. Many of the items that he has questioned this afternoon are for purposes which perhaps go further than any others towards promoting good will and good relations between countries. Our legations have been instruments for avoiding conflicts, for getting at the root of difficulties at their inception. The amount that will be expended in connection with the coronation will be a means, I am perfectly sure, of bringing together representative groups from all parts of the empire in a way which will further effect cooperation and good will among them. I think we must view these questions from the larger point of view that we are a full .grown nation, with not only the opportunity of fulfilling the obligations of a nation but with a certain pride in the way in which we do it.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Send farmers and fishermen and textile workers, then, instead of sending soldiers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: May I say to the hon. member that I believe the young men who are in our defence forces, who are prepared to give, if need be, their lives at a time as critical in the affairs of the w'orld as the present time, are deserving, whether they serve in the air force or the naval forces or the militia, of all the encouragement and all the honour that this parliament can give them. I resent strongly the imputation that a man who is prepared to offer his life in the service and for the protection of his country, on behalf of those who are unable to defend themselves, is not discharging an all-important function for the nation to-day.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: I made no such imputation. I said that we should send as our delegates persons who represent the different classes of our people. The Prime Minister has stated that we should send people who would promote peace. My suggestion was that if we were sincere in our desire to promote peace we might well send representatives of farmers and fishermen and miners as well as sending soldiers.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: You said, instead of sending soldiers.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: All we are sending represent one class. I suggest to the Prime Minister that it would be equally possible for me to say that he insinuated that the farmers and the miners and so on were not the people who were at the foundations of our life. I do not charge he did say that, but I resent his suggestion that there was any justification for the statement he imputed to me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: May I say that in the militia service there will be many taken from the ranks of the artisans of this country; there will be farmers, miners and representatives of other trades and callings. I was not making any insinuations. My hon. friend remarked that we had better not send soldiers, and I was trying to point out that in a world such as we are in to-day those who are offering their services to the state as soldiers are deserving of all the recognition we can give them.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY TO THE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I doubt whether the Prime Minister's statement is altogether correct, that the people of Canada are greatly interested in seeing that Canada makes as good a showing as South Africa and New Zealand and Australia. There are thousands of people across

Divorce in British Columbia-Mr. Green
the dominion who are not particularly anxious about the kind of showing we make, but who are face to face with their greatest problem, that of making a living. When passing expenditures of this sort, and one to which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) referred the other evening, this parliament should bear in mind that there are people in Canada, people in the province and the constituency from which I come, who are living on relief grants of from $6.50 to nineteen or twenty dollars per month, people who are receiving five dollars in their home when they are expecting the arrival of a child, people unable to get eye glasses or proper dental or medical care. To such it must be a striking contrast that we pass votes, one of $35,000 for the delegation to the coronation, one of $197,000 for a contingent to attend the coronation, one of $65,000 to decorate buildings across the dominion with flags at the coronation, one of $40,000 for the imperial conference. If we omit the item for the conference, there is a total of around $300,000, and it is in striking contrast to the fact that to the people I have mentioned we dole out a few cents here and a few cents there, sometimes after a most humiliating examination of their circumstances. When the Prime Minister feels that we are particularly worried over the matter of keeping up with the other members of the British commonwealth of nations, may I remind him that there are thousands of people who are much more interested in seeing that we properly discharge our responsibilities to our people who are in need throughout the dominion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOE APPEAL TO PROVINCIAL COURT OF APPEAL IN DIVORCE AND MATRIMONIAL CAUSES

speechtext:
Mr. H. C. GREEN (Vancouver South) moved the second reading of Bill No. 15, to provide for appeal to the court of appeal of the province of British Columbia in divorce and matrimonial causes.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to provide for an appeal in divorce causes in British Columbia to the appeal court of that province. At the present time, in divorce and matrimonial causes, the only appeal in that province from the trial court, which is called the supreme
court of British Columbia, is direct to the privy council, which means in actual practice that except for very wealthy people there is n.o appeal at all. This is an, anomalous situation, for in every other province in which the courts have and exercise jurisdiction in divorce matters there is an appeal to the appellate court of the particular province. Let me make it quite clear at the outset that the purpose of this bill is not to give a new or wider jurisdiction to grant divorces in British Columbia. It is merely to give power to our appeal court to review decrees which are made by the trial court.
Hon. members may wondeT how it happens that the trial court, known as the supreme court of British Columbia, has jurisdiction in divorce causes, while the court of appeal, which is a senior court, has not such jurisdiction. It does seem a ridiculous situation. It came about in this way: When the colony of British Columbia entered confederation in 1871, there was a trial court known even then as the supreme court, but there was no appellate court. At that time the law of England as of November 19, 1858, was in force so far as it was not inapplicable through local circumstances. This law of England included the divorce law of England, which accordingly was in force in the colony of British Columbia. Upon that colony entering confederation, the law-making power in so far as divorce matters were concerned passed by section 91 (26) of the British North America Act from the colony to the dominion, where it has ever since reposed. But the dominion passed no divorce legislation, so under section 129 of the British North America Act the divorce law of England remained in force in British Columbia, and it so remains to this day.
In 1877, a few years after the province entered confederation, it was held by the supreme court of British Columbia that this divorce law of England was still in effect in the province and that the supreme court of British Columbia had power to grant divorces. Those who would care to check the decision will find it in Sharp v. Sharp, reported in 1 B.C. Reports at page 25.
So much for the trial court. The appeal court has not been so fortunate. As the population of the province grew, the need for a court of review became apparent, so the provincial legislature passed legislation setting up a court of review, which was known as the full court, and giving to that full court ths power to review every judgment, decree or order made by a judge of the supreme court. One might think that was wide enough to give an appeal in divorce causes. But in 1891 the full court itself held that it had no
712	COMMONS
Divorce in British Columbia-Mr. Green
power to hear appeals in divorce matters, because under the British North America Act the provincial legislature had no power to confer divorce jurisdiction upon any court. That remains the law to this day. It was confirmed within recent years by the present court of appeal for British Columbia, which has replaced the full court, and also confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Claman v. Claman, the decision of the appeal court of British Columbia being found in (1925) 35 B.C. Reports, at page 137, and the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in (1926) 68 Supreme Court Reports, at page 4.
I should like to quote an extract from the judgment of Chief Justice Macdonald of the appeal court of British Columbia in this case. He said:
In the early history of this province, the courts considered that the English Divorce Act was in force here, and that an appeal would lie only to the privy council. Since that time appeals have invariably been made to the privy council and not to the court of appeal of the province, so that that became the established or recognized rule and has remained such for many years unquestioned.
That, of course, leaves the only appeal from the trial court an appeal direct to the privy council. In every other province in which the courts have and exercise jurisdiction in divorce causes, there is an appeal to the appellate court of the province. For example, in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick I believe the divorce laws which they had as colonies before confederation remain in force, and there is an appeal. In Ontario, where there was no divorce law before confederation, this parliament by chapter 14 of 1930 declared the English divorce law as of July 15, 1870, to be in force in the province. And this parliament went further and gave the Ontario courts jurisdiction to hear divorce causes, which included, of course, the right to hear appeals. In the three prairie provinces privy council decisions have established that the English divorce law of July 15, 1870 is in force, and decisions of the provincial appeal courts within the last few years have established their own right to hear appeals. British Columbia remains the only province where there is no such right to hear appeals. In that province the court of appeal can hear appeals of all other kinds; for instance they can hear an appeal from a county court judgment in the sum of $100 or over, but they cannot hear an appeal in such vital matters as a decree dissolving a marriage, eul order for the custody of the children of that marriage, or an order for alimony.

For some time this position has been recognized as unsound by the barristers and solicitors in British Columbia and by the benchers of the law society there. The law society at its annual meeting two years ago passed a resolution requesting that provision be made for appeals to the court of appeal in British Columbia, and the benchers of the law society on April 6 of last year passed the following resolution:
That the benchers request that provision be made for appeals from divorce matters to the court of appeal in the same manner as in civil cases, and that copies of the resolution be sent to the Minister of Justice, Hon. Ian Mackenzie, and the Attorney General of British Columbia.
. Now the provincial legislature cannot provide for such appeals because the British North America Act gives the dominion parliament exclusive authority in divorce matters, so an appeal is impossible unless it is provided for by this parliament. We are not asking that divorce jurisdiction be conferred on the provincial courts as was done in the case of Ontario, because our supreme court already has that jurisdiction. We are merely asking that the right of appeal be provided.
The question is of great importance. After all, the setting aside of a marriage is a serious matter; deciding as to the custody of children of that marriage is a serious matter; and yet in British Columbia a marriage can be set aside and the custody of the children determined without any right of appeal except to the privy council, which in the great majority of cases means no appeal at all. As a result I fear that our people think that divorces are easy to get; I fear that they do not give the serious consideration to the question of divorce which it merits. I suggest that it is not fair or wise that there should be no appeal in British Columbia when there is an appeal in all the other provinces exercising divorce jurisdiction.
I ask that the bill be passed, because 1 think it is really constructive legislation meeting a great need. It is put forward without any idea of partisanship, and, as I have said, simply to meet a condition which must be remedied. This parliament is the only body that can provide the remedy.

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act so as to constitute committees instead of one advisory committee, and to appropriate the necessary moneys for the continuance and extension of the work under the Act for the fiscal years 1937-38 to 1939-40 inclusive.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

Perhaps the better course would be to have the minister give the explanation now with respect to the resolution, so that questions may be asked, rather than to enter upon a discussion before it is taken up by the committee.

The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act is a short act passed in 1935. It was brought into being as a result of conditions which prevailed over a section of western Canada which includes about twenty municipalities in Manitoba, about one hundred and fifty in Saskatchewan and probably one hundred in Alberta, an area which has been affected by particularly dry seasons during the past seven years. The act provided for the setting up of an advisory committee. That advisory committee was to be composed of representatives of different organizations and corporations in Canada. The act provided also for the doing of certain work in western Canada, the Department of Agriculture, which under the bill was designated as the department responsible, acting on the advice of the committee which was set up under section 3. This was in order that certain things might be done, such as providing supplies of water for farmers attempting to raise live stock in that area and for tree culture, in order to protect lands against blowing, if possible, in certain areas; the promotion of strip farming; the regrassing of some of the lands that had been found unsuitable for wheat growing, and anything else that might be found in the interests of the farmers of that area or that might rehabilitate them as farmers.
In order to carry out the intentions of the act it was provided under section 8 that during the first year, which was 1935-36, a sum not exceeding three-quarters of a million dollars should be provided for expenditure in that area, and that during the succeeding four years a sum not exceeding one million dollars a year should be available for expenditure. Members of the house will recall that a year ago we voted 8750,000 as the amount that would be available for expenditure. I may say that during the two years that have gone by less than 8850,000 has been spent. The amount that was set aside for the first year was not exhausted, nor was the amount set aside for the second year. This was largely because of the fact that the work was in the experimental stage, and it was not thought wise to proceed more rapidly with the expenditure of money than our experience would warrant. Now, however, we feel that we have gained sufficient experience in the work to have more definite ideas as to what ought to be done and as to the amounts of money which may be necessary in order to carry out the original intentions of the act.
We also feel that in carrying out some of the work which is contemplated it will be necessary to have more than one advisory committee. The committee that was created

Farm Rehabilitation Act
under the original bill advised on matters of general policy, but we think it wise to have, in some of the local areas, advisory committees that will be more familiar with what is being carried out in those areas and that can give advice which probably will be more advantageous to the department. Therefore we are suggesting that section 3 be amended in order to make it possible for us to have more than one committee and so that we shall not be confined to the appointment of the representatives of any particular organizations in forming such committees. Just in passing I may say that the members of those committees act without remuneration.
Then it is intended by amending section 4, to widen to some extent the work that may be undertaken under this act. The experience of those living to the south of the international boundary line in dealing with similar problems brought to our minds the thought that something similar might be done north of the boundary line, altered in some measure so as to meet the different conditions which exist in this country. In other words, we are hoping to make use in a larger way of the available water supplies and to provide artificially water supplies for the purpose of assisting in resettling people in this vast area. In addition to that, we hope to take advantage of the experience of the government of Saskatchewan in connection with what is called a community ranch, which is operated more in the form of a community pasture, available to the people of a considerable area to the north of the Saskatchewan river, and which is known as the Matador ranch. Similar experiments have been conducted in the states immediately to the south, though some of them have differed slightly from what has been done in Saskatchewan. Some experimental work has been done in Alberta in making available to farmers who are settled in the drought area larger areas for pasture, and we hope to enlarge our work to assist further development of undertakings of that sort.
The only other important amendment is the one having to do with the supply of funds for carrying out the purposes of the act. We fee! that the government could accomplish more without the limitation of a million dollars which is contained in the bill. As the act now stands, a million dollars is the limit which may be spent in any one year, and we are asking for this change in spite of the fact that we did not think it wise to spend even three-quarters of a million last year or the year before. We think that with the experience we now have we can probably spend more than a million dollars during the
year, if we can get such an estimate adopted by this house, and 'it is in order to provide more than that amount that I am asking for this amendment.
Those are the important changes to be made in the act if the present bill passes, and if any other information is desired, I shall be pleased to try to furnish it.
May I say it is not the intention to set up municipal committees. Perhaps I should have explained that.
It is proposed to place a limitation upon the size, is it?

The intention is to maintain the committee now operating, and it is just possible that we may require in a ranching area a special committee of ranchers, or in a wheat growing area a special committee of wheat growers, to deal with questions peculiar to a particular part of the country.

The very reasons I have given are responsible for the personnel as I have read it. It was felt that there was a danger of self interest dominating judgments with respect to policies, and that the wisdom and experience of men of divers occupations concerned with areas some of which were fit only for grazing and ranching, and some of which were fit for farming, might result in the formulation of plans which would be more conducive to the well-being of the whole.
I make these statements only because I would hesitate to support any proposal which might bring about a measure of friction between the central committee, to which I have referred, and any committee which might feel a deep and abiding concern about one matter, and one only. That is, you might have a committee which would be concerned only about the farming area, and another only about the ranching area, and you would have the age old struggle as to what constitutes a purely ranching area or a purely farming area. For instance, I think there is no difficulty to-day in getting at least seventy-five per cent of people affected to say that areas which were opened for agricultural settlement never should have been so opened, and that they should have been retained as ranching lands. The problem is not one which is wholly singular to Canada. It has arisen in other countries as well. I believe it has arisen in Australia. I suggest that the

Farm Rehabilitation Act
danger of a conflict between what I describe as the national interest dealing with the national problem and the personal interest dealing with the purely domestic or local problem is one which must be ever present.
I assume the government is taking discretionary authority, and does not make it in any sense obligatory that the committee should be set up, because I apprehend that if it were obligatory that it be set up, there might be conflict such as would not be beneficial to the interests of any.
There comes then the question as to the measures to be taken. I for one at the proper time would like to hear a complete statement by the minister as to what has been done and what he hopes may be done. If there is to be provision in the appropriation bill, that would seem to be the appropriate time to make such a statement. I confess that in looking at the situation from my angle I have been a little depressed, and have found it most difficult to get much encouragement from any reliable source as to the method which can be adopted to bring about a solution of this difficulty, short of providence once more smiling upon the land with steady rains.
