I am deeply interested in this matter. When the proposals came before us in 1935 they followed the drought of 1934. When that statute was being prepared, it was quite apparent that we were going to have a dry season in 1935, dry from the standpoint not of lack of rain, but of lack of moisture from snow. There was no accumulation of waters resulting from melting snow and the impounding of it in any part of the country. It is not a matter of importance, but I cannot say that I view with great approval the question of authorizing expenditures in excess of $1,000,000 a year. One million dollars a year is a substantial sum of money. I thought possibly the minister was going to suggest that he was going to amend the statute by striking out the provisions with reference to any period beyond this year and to make in the estimates such appropriations as experience warranted in the light of the knowledge which he would then possess. The statute, as it is now, reads as follows:
For the purposes of this act the sum of seven hundred aud fifty thousand dollars shall he appropriated and paid out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada during the fiscal year 1935-36 and for each fiscal year for a further period of four years a sum not exceeding $1,000,000 per annum as may be necessary to continue and extend the work undertaken under this act.
I understand the minister to say that he thinks $1,000,000 is a limitation that should not be imposed upon the expenditures contemplated by the act. He is in possession of information that induces him to believe that he can usefully expend over $1,000,000. In view of the position taken by the leader of the government with reference to the absolute necessity of including any such appropriation in the supply bill, I suggest that instead of including it in this bill, which would be superfluous, expenditures be authorized up to March 31, 1938, at a figure which the minister may regard as being reasonably satisfactory, having regard to the knowledge which he possesses. In view of the position taken by the government as to the desirability, nay the necessity, from their standpoint, of any provision of this kind being included in the appropriation bill, which we refer to as the estimates when before the committee of the house before being
Farm Rehabilitation Act

embodied in the bill, it would perhaps be desirable to repeal this section in its entirety and make provision for a single year. The government could then adopt the policy which they urged strenuously in days gone by and ask for an additional sum of money in the light of the experience derived from the operations of the past year.
I hope, when the appropriation is before the committee, the minister will prepare himself to give us as complete a statement as possible of what has been done. I say this because I believe in every part of Canada and in many parts of the world eyes are being directed to what is being done in western Canada in an effort to bring back these lands to their former fertility. For instance, this matter is of tremendous importance to this province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To our whole economic structure.

On one occasion I said that there was not a citizen of this country who was not interested in it, and I still believe that to be true. When the appropriation is before the committee, I hope the minister will have prepared himself to make as full a statement as the facts warrant with respect to what has been done and with respect to the possible results of the efforts that may be made. For one, I would greatly appreciate it.
I think there are many people in this country who are deeply concerned about the problem which arises from the fact that about three hundred municipalities in western Canada are suffering from a lack of moisture to such an extent as to make farming operations not only unprofitable but impossible. In many instances this condition has compelled the rancher to move his herds from the areas affected. I can conceive of no problem at the moment that is of greater importance to Canada. The government with which I was associated was responsible for initiating this movement and we are perhaps more anxious than one can readily understand to see that some results accrue from the efforts that were initiated and carried out with small expenditures. I am advised that it is well that these expenditures were not larger for this would involve the loss of the moneys which might have been expended for that purpose.
I am not unmindful of the fact that south of us there exists a situation not unlike our own. Although it has existed for a shorter period, it has been acute. The methods adopted there to deal with the situation are similar to those we have used. Consideration has been given to strip farming and to the question of the cultivation of certain grasses. In the desert

areas of one of the dominions I found that they have a particular kind of grass which has been found exceedingly valuable. I made inquiry of the Department of Agriculture with respect to it, and I was informed that it would make an excellent binder and is of fair nutritive value. I cannot say whether it would bring about any satisfactory results in a soil such as ours, which is largely alluvial as compared with that of the other dominions.
Hon. members should visualize a situation in which the grass binder which covered this area has been cut to pieces by man's efforts. The soil has just become like talcum powder. When exposed to wind it blows about like snow on a winter's day. I saw one farm, which at one time produced the largest quantity of wheat per acre in that locality, covered with great drifts of earth as high as the desk in front of me. There were no visible crops and there had been none for years. How this situation is to be met is a, problem that faces the government of this day. Something must be done to recover the economic strength and the fortunes of the people who occupy this country. At one time these people had good homes and fine outbuildings, and they thought themselves to be in circumstances beyond the possibility of any disaster that might come to them in their lifetime. As the minister has said, some of these people are to-day on relief.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A great number of them.

A great number of them. Under those circumstances anything we can do by timely suggestion, by support of any action to strengthen the hand of the government in dealing with this problem, we shall do, not only because it is our duty to do it, but because we all realize how important is the problem from the standpoint of the maintenance of the integrity of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that I should seize this opportunity to offer a few remarks in regard to conditions which prevail in western Canada. I feel that the magnitude of the terrible disaster which has overtaken that portion of our dominion cannot be too often impressed upon this house, and I believe the people of western Canada will be very grateful indeed for the remarks which have been made to-night by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett).
While I do not live in the dried-out area, yet it is coming pretty close even to Portage la Prairie. While we had a crop last year, one did not need to go over fifteen miles west before one ran into the dried-out area. I had the opportunity to drive through that

Farm Rehabilitation Act
dried-out portion of Manitoba two years ago, and to see for myself the conditions that exist there, and so true is the picture which has been painted by the right hon. leader of the opposition that one's imagination can scarcely grasp it. One has to see that country for oneself. A person will drive hundreds of miles and not see a green shoot anywhere. Even the leaves on the trees are dead, and the shrubbery along the road has died off. Even the gophers and the grasshoppers have left those districts, for want of something to eat.
As a farmer and from my experience as a live stock breeder, I should like to suggest to the minister, when he brings down his legislation for the rehabilitation of that area, to have some regard also for the live stock industry and what it means to that part of the country. We must all recognize that wheat growing in a portion of western Canada must give way to the raising of live stock, and the remarks I want to make to-night bear especially upon the beef cattle industry.
I assume the government is going to make some expenditure in providing capital for the dried-out area, and I want to impress upon them the necessity of procuring good stock, especially good sires. The quality of our live stock has depreciated during the last seven or eight years, and there is a reason for it. People have not had the money to buy good sires. At the recent cattle-breeders' meeting held in Regina, the prevalence of scrub bulls which infest western Canada, and especially that dried-out area, was declared to be alarming, and the cattle breeders are asking the government to furnish more money so that the farmers may be able to procure better sires and to build up a better quality of cattle. Realizing the possibilities of the British market for good cattle and the possibilities of the American market-we know what these markets demand because we have men both in the United States and in Great Britain whose business it is to find out what the pepple demand, and I am aware the officers of the department know the quality of cattle that these markets demand-I believe it is only good business on the part of the department to see, when they are building up the live stock industry in that devastated area, that any money spent in that direction will be spent especially for the purpose of procuring good sires. I want to impress that upon the minister and upon the committee tonight because, from my experience in the business for a good many years I know the value of good sires, and I know what will happen to any live stock grower if he persists
in using poor ones. The government, I understand, realize that the farmers must desist from wheat growing and that facilities must be provided for rearing live stock, and I say that facilities must be provided because they do not exist at the present time.
Owing to the drought and other conditions, such as draining the country, we find that there is not enough water even for the animals. The government realizes this, and is providing dugouts, damming up streams, and conserving the water supply of that area. This is an indication that they intend to rehabilitate the live stock industry in the area.
Just before resuming my seat I would again impress upon the minister the necessity of providing good sires, and sires of the proper beef type if any pretence of raising good beef cattle is being made.

Mr. Chairman, might I suggest to the minister that when he brings down his legislation for the rehabilitation of the prairie farms, he be prepared not only to tell the house what has been done and what it is proposed to do, but that he give the house a survey of the actual conditions which exist and of the problem which really arises out of those conditions. This is very largely a new House of Commons, and although in the last house very much was said about the conditions then arising in western Canada, this House of Commons is unfamiliar with the problem. Moving around eastern Canada I find that people do not appreciate the vastness of the area which is affected and the tremendous problem which faces not merely western Canada but the whole of Canada because of conditions in the prairie provinces. Very few members can realize an experience which I am sure the Minister of Agriculture has had as well as I, of driving for a whole day across a couple of hundred miles of territory in Saskatchewan, and during the whole day not seeing our radiator caps except occasionally through the dust that was caused by the soil erosion. Yet people are living there under such conditions.
The leader of the opposition said that in some parts there has been no crop for five years. I know of districts that have had no crop for seven years. I do not believe, however, that all these lands are by any means lost. There are areas-I do not think they are very large-where the top soil has drifted away, and where the erosion has gone to such an extent that you will see holes six and eight feet deep blown out of the surface. But, as I say, those areas are, I think, comparatively small. If proper steps are taken,
Farm Rehabilitation Act

I believe the country can be largely rehabilitated, but in my opinion the rehabilitation will involve not only a land rehabilitation plan but also a resettlement plan. When the minister brings down the legislation, might I suggest that he give us some of the figures from the recent soil surveys which have been made in our province. The university of Saskatchewan has done a great deal of work along these lines, as the minister told the house the other afternoon, and we know something of the soil constituents, of the moisture deficiency, of the loss of fibre, of the future possibilities of that vast area comprising over three hundred municipalities, now suffering from various degrees of drought. If we are to consider this measure intelligently, we should have that background. Not only has the minister the required data available, but, as the head of a government in Saskatchewan during several recent years, and with his long experience of administration on the prairies, I do not think there should be anyone better fitted than the present Minister of Agriculture to give the house authentic information. I believe that we should have this information and that the people of Canada, through the minister, should be informed of the condition that really faces us, because, like the leader of the opposition, I have been sometimes depressed and very gloomy concerning it.
When I went west last summer, I drove through the United States, and for a thousand miles from Minneapolis to Regina. As one saw the crops withering, and realized1 that one oould go another six hundred miles west and south of Regina and see the same condition everywhere, one wondered what was going to become of the country that appeared to some of us twenty-five years or more ago as among the most beautiful pieces of prairie land which could be found anywhere in the world. I think it would be not only interesting but useful to the house to have that information, because men and women in the stricken area are suffering; children too are suffering. As I said the other afternoon, the schools axe sometimes1 cold. We are told authoritatively that last winter for days on end some schools did not have fuel enough to keep the temperature above freezing point. Teachers are working for, ten dollars a month. There are people on the farms who have not seen much in the way of money for many months, indeed for years, and there are people without proper clothing. Although the people of eastern Canadh have responded splendidly to the appeals which have been made, and we express to them our thanks whenever we get the opportunity, nevertheless that is not going to solve the problem. The
IMr. Coldwell.]
problem remains unsolved, and I suggest to the minister that when the legislation comes down, it would1 be well for this house to have presented to it a clear picture of the problem in western Canada as it affects the entire dominion. Incidentally, I do not think it can be solved in a short time; a long range program will have to 'be inaugurated by this parliament.

I do not want to attempt to shorten the discussion, but I should like to take advantage of the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and also by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, to say that I intend to move this bill to second reading for Thursday, and I shall attempt between now and Thursday to prepare for the house not only a review of the situation as we know it in the department and as I knew it in the province before I came to the department, but also a review of what past governments have spent in that country, and, through past governments having made these expenditures, of what people in other parts of Canada have really done in order to assist in rebuilding not only the soil of that country but the morale of the people themselves. It would be good for all of us to have a complete picture of that side of the whole experience. If, after that is presented to the house, there is not sufficient information1 to form a background) for any discussions that it is desired to have of the whole problem, another opportunity will arise, as was suggested by the leader of the opposition, when the estimate is brought before the house setting forth the amount of money the government desires to make available for expenditure in that area this year.
With regard to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, I wish only to say I am a little afraid1 that setting up a sum for one year without anything in the form of a statutory provision for an expenditure in at least two succeeding years would not be an improvement on the present act.

You would be just as
well off.

Well, I would rather see no definite limiting dates at all for the time being. I may Say that the United States- although I speak from memory I think I am correct-is dealing with an area of country which is not materially greater than the area which is affected in western Canada; perhaps its situation has been a little more serious in some years than it has been in western Canada, but the area is not materially larger-

More densely settled.

Farm Rehabilitation Act

The minister presides over a department that is spending $7,500,000 on commissions and! committees. Coming from the prairie provinces, he is very fond of this committee and commission business, but I may tell him that in the United States, with 130.000,000 people, similar work is handled by one man only, Mr. Hopkins, and they did not have the bungling and muddling that have gone on in the last six months in connection with the administration of this particular farm rehabilitation act. I have heard! and read a good deal about it; it has been very badly handled by those who have had charge of it in the last year. The minister now proposes to have a vaster committee system than before to handle this vote. Everyone wants to see that the poor people on the prairies who have suffered shall get every possible assistance. It is to come, no doubt, out of the revenues of the consolidated fund and income derived from the industrial provinces of Ontario and Quebec, which pay about eighty per cent of the taxes.
Hon. members will recall the rosy picture which was painted by the minister in the last few days of last session, when he indicated that everything was going to grow like the flowers upon the prairie. His committee of one hundred will soon expand to two hundred. This committee system, as I see it, is against the whole principle of responsible government. This is a department which is spending seven and a half million dollars for deputy ministers and their apostles to go all over this country from coast to coast. I think the time has come for us to get back to responsible government instead of this government by committees inside and out. Why does the minister not look around the country for another famous dynamic figure like Mr. Purvis who was to get all the unemployed on the payrolls in the industrial cities and has yet found no jobs. As one who comes from Toronto, an industrial city, I believe-this is a protectionist doctrine-in helping these unemployed to the utmost credit of the country, but let us help these poor people on the prairies too. I believe in equality of treatment. Let us play the game fairly, as the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) said the other night. He always plays the game fairly himself, and he knows a great deal about agriculture. The time is coming when this farm rehabilitation scheme must be applied to all the provinces; I would not limit it to the prairies, although I would give them every support. But last summer I saw farmers in the province I come from, when the temperature was 108 to 110 degrees, suffering very nearly as much as those on the prairies.
There should be an end to all this committee system. I am sick and tired of the way in which this parliament is appointing commissions and committees, and the next year we get a report and we find it is not as rosy a picture as has been painted. We see the mistakes that have been made in rehabilitation schemes in the United States. I fail to see where the new system of committees, we do not know how many, will produce any better results than the old. There should be equality of treatment; the minister's department should look after the other provinces where farmers are suffering in much the same way as they are in his own province.

Would the minister kindly
outline the operation of a community cattle ranch, as carried on at the Matador, I think he said.

The Matador ranch is situated in the bow of the Saskatchewan river northwest of Moose Jaw. At the time that territory ceased to operate as a ranch the provincial government took over the area, fenced it and put a man in charge, and the people of the community round about put their cattle in, paying a fee of so much a head. I understand that ranch has paid more than the running expenses; it has cost the government nothing from the time it was started. It has given accommodation to the people of the surrounding area for pasturing their cattle, relieving them of the overhead for maintaining and carrying extra lands themselves. Anything that is done along that line will naturally have to be done in cooperation
Farm Rehabilitation Act

with the provincial governments, because they now own the lands and control the operation of them. Anything done would be done by the province, probably with some assistance from Ottawa in the way of direction and otherwise in connection with the stocking.
What is the size of this area?
About three or four townships, I think. It is irregular in form, the river forming the southern boundary. A township contains thirty-six square miles.
Is that ranch growing its own hay and winter feed?

Well the stock is mostly taken out in the winter and taken home by the farmers. The stock belongs not to any one person but to scores of persons round about, and they look after putting up the feed for the winter.

I should like to ask the minister when bringing down this report to have in mind the enormous wealth which those prairies have produced during the last thirty-five years. I say that for the special benefit of our comrades from Ontario. Had the west not poured out that great wealth, there would have been very little manufacturing in Ontario.

I should like to say a word to encourage the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). He does not need to worry about that great move he made in introducing the prairie farm rehabilitation scheme. There is abundance of water, especially in the foothill areas on the east side of the Rocky mountains. There is great opportunity for storing that water; the possibilities seem to me to be well nigh limitless. I should like to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for his ambition in reaching out and setting no limit within reason to the amount of money which he will spend as he deems wise. There are tremendous possibilities. We should remember this also, that although we have not been in this country long enough to be able to be certain, it appears that the weather goes in cycles. In my constituency we have had great scarcity of moisture during the last several years until we began to think we were deserted entirely by the deities controlling precipitation. But now we have more snow there than we know what to do with, and it looks as if we are going to have abundance of moisture in the coming season. So I feel that we need not be greatly alarmed by this talk about an insoluble problem. If we go at it in a systematic, persistent way it will be solved. The prairie farm rehabilitation scheme is a good one which will give excellent results in the days to come.

Supply-Agriculture-Cold Storage
There are quite a few questions I should like to ask the minister but I shall leave them until the estimates are brought down. I just want to stress the point that drought is really a permanent condition. There is no use in hoping that a change of climate will take place in the near future and bring about a change in these conditions, because we can go right back to 1857 and find that we have had to face this problem ever since that time, so it is not likely that these conditions will change within any short period.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Gardiner thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 18, to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext: The Cold Storage Act, as hon. members know, provides that when a cold storage plant is constructed according to the regulations laid down by the department, which cold storage plant is to be made available to the public, the federal government will pay thirty per cent of the cost, and the payment of that thirty per cent is spread over five years.
Cost of construction?
Yes, cost of construction. The payment of that thirty per cent is spread over a five year period. This money is to provide for the amounts that may have to be paid under the act.
Is that a permanent provision in the act?
Yes.
That is, until the act is changed, governments will always provide a thirty per cent subsidy for the erection of cold storage plants?
Yes, so long as the government leaves the act on the statute books.
The reduction is due to the fact that some subsidies have expired.

The real reason is that at this time of the year it is almost impossible to estimate the amount which may be necessary. In other years, when the session has run on until the month of June, we have followed the practice of bringing down supplementary estimates. This vote is identical with the one passed a year ago, but the additional amount was covered by a supplementary brought in later in the session.
How much was actually paid out in the last fiscal year?
In round figures, $84,000.
Why is only about half that amount provided this year?

For the reason I gave a moment ago. It is impossible at this time of the year to estimate exactly how many applications will be made throughout the year. Later in past sessions we have been able to estimate more nearly the amount, and have brought down a supplementary to cover it.

Before the Department of Agriculture agrees to granting a subsidy, are the plans and specifications submitted to the department, or does the company which proposes to build simply go ahead and build, and then make application for the subsidy? In other words, is there any regulation or control over the erection of plants or cold storage warehouses?

According to the regulations, plans have to accompany applications, and inspections are made. Not all applications are passed by the department. In many instances they are sent back and the applicants are asked to make provision in addition to that shown in the original plans. I brought down a special supplementary last year to take care of two plants which in previous years had started operations before making application to the government. It took them about three years to satisfy the government that they had provided facilities sufficient to warrant the payment of the grant.
Suppose in a district there is more than sufficient accommodation to take care of the requirements; in such case would the government give a subsidy for another cold storage plant?
No; the government would not give a grant if in its opinion the building was too costly or of dimensions greater than required to satisfy the existing conditions.

Do I understand the minister to say that when the federal department makes a grant for the erection of these buildings, they are then turned over to the operating company, or does the government make grants in addition to those made in connection with the erection and equipment of the building?

The grants are paid over five years, and under certain conditions additional grants are paid. But the plants are always subject to regulation with regard to charges, and are open to the public for storage purposes, as long as they are operated.
In that event the federal government will not derive any benefit from charges made for storage?
No; the federal government does not get any financial returns. In the first instance the intention was to encourage the construction of cold storage plants.
Do we understand from the minister that in some cases the department gives more than thirty per cent?
No more than thirty per cent is paid on any plant that is built. It is only when an addition is made to the space that another thirty per cent is paid.
If an addition is added, the department adds another thirty per cent?
Yes.
Have certain of these companies gone out of existence? Are all the cold storage warehouses being operated at a profit? What is done in the case of a warehouse which is not making any profit?

So far as the department knows, they are all operating. Some of them are operating in connection with trading concerns and probably are not operating exactly in accordance with the provisions set up at the time they were first built.

I have been struck with the apparent discrepancy in the number of cold storage plants in the different provinces. I believe there are five in Prince Edward Island, two in New Brunswick and twenty in Nova Scotia. Is there any particular reason for there being only a few plants in some provinces white there are more in others?

The number of cold storage plants in a particular province depends largely upon the necessity for cold storage in that province. Where fruit and fish and dairy products are largely produced, naturally cold storage is needed. British Columbia has a large number of storage warehouses, as have Ontario and Nova Scotia.

Dairying, $290,000.

I wish to call the attention of the minister to a condition which I think has more to do with the quality of our cheese exported than anything else, and that is the practice of shipping our cheeses too green. There is a regulation that the graders are not supposed to grade a cheese until it is eight days old, but any regulation that might be passed compelling a cheese maker to hold cheeses in his factory for eight days, or whatever other time might be specified, does not remedy the evil for this reason:	It
is not the shipping of the cheese, it is the boxing of the cheese that causes the trouble. If green cheeses are placed in boxes before they are sufficiently dried, the moisture causes a mould that discolours the cheese and very often causes a soft rind. Many of our small cheese factories have not enough shelf-room to hold more than two or three days' make of cheese, and if they are compelled to hold cheeses more than a week in the factory, they simply box them up, put them in the comer and leave them there over the week. These cheeses should be left on the shelves without being boxed, and should be turned every day for a week. One exporter told me that he had worked up a splendid trade for cheese for a certain firm in the old country, but that he could not supply them with these mouldy cheeses which had been boxed before they were properly dried out, because while the mould on the outside very often does not deteriorate the cheese itself, it certainly spoils its appearance.
There is another matter that is bothering the dairymen at the present time. Some years ago parliament passed legislation prohibiting the importation of oleomargarine. That prohibition was of great benefit to the dairy farmers, but its advantage is being nulli-

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
fied to a certain extent by the importation of vegetable oils. Vegetable oils are coming in and being manufactured into shortening and other ingredients used in baking and cooking, and these are taking the place of butter. We manufacture in this country on an average ten million pounds of butter a year more than we can consume, and for that ten million pounds of butter we must find a market outside Canada. These vegetable oils which are coming in are coming from countries with a low scale of wages where the standard of living is very low. They are bought very cheaply, and after they are refined, the better class of oils goes into shortenings and other ingredients used in cooking and baking, and they take the place of our butter and lard. This displaces the consumption of our own butter and animal fats, as the shortenings are frequently used in the place of butter. The lower grade oils are made into soaps. About eighty million pounds of vegetable oils are imported annually, and the importation in the last two years has increased by twenty-four million pounds, so that they have become a serious contender with butter in this country.
I would point out to the minister that the United States has protected its dairymen by imposing a duty of 4J cents a pound on vegetable oils entering that country, while they enter Canada free. That duty has turned the tide of vegetable oils into the Canadian market. I would ask the minister to take this matter into his serious consideration because our dairymen to-day are becoming alarmed at the ever-increasing sales sf shortenings which are made from vegetable oils and which are taking the place of our butter and animal fats.

An application with respect to vegetable oils, has been made to the tariff board and is now receiving its consideration, so I do not think I am in a position to say that any further consideration can be given the matter at the moment.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which I think ought to have been brought to the attention of the house sooner. On the previous day the agriculture estimates were considered in the house the evening papers carried the announcement that the whole Department of Agriculture was to be reorganized and that there were to be three main branches: production, research and marketing. It came as rather a surprise to me and, I think, to other hon. members, that this had not been mentioned before the agriculture estimates were considered.

I should like first of all to commend the action of the minister for choosing the men he did to head these branches. Doctor Archibald and Mr. Rothwell are well known to agriculture generally throughout the dominion. I do not think there is a better authority on agricultural matters in Canada to-day than Doctor Archibald. The administration of his department in the past has been very excellent indeed. The same may be said for Mr. Rothwell. He has made himself deservedly popular with the live stock men of this country. I am glad the minister has seen fit to retain the services of these two men in the department.
It is difficult to understand how the estimates are to be allocated after this reorganization takes place. Take, for instance, this branch of dairying. We have the production activities, the research branch and the marketing branch. Just how this vote is to be divided among the different branches is difficult for me to understand. Again, as far as the marketing branch is concerned, if I am correctly informed or if my ideas are correct, marketing within the province is solely within the jurisdiction of the province. The supervision of marketing outside the country or interprovincial marketing has largely been, as I understand the matter, the work of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I think the minister would be wise, in view of the reorganization, to make a statement as to how these estimates are to be divided, so that we may discuss them more intelligently.

I had intended to discuss fully the matters referred to upon the vote for marketing, which is the last vote, on page 19. If hon. members will permit of it being done at that time it would be preferable, I think, to starting in to explain the matter at five minutes to eleven o'clock.
Then I think the minister should let this item stand until we have a chance to hear his explanation.

Well, it really has very little to do with this item. The marketing item covers the whole matter under consideration; anything that is to be taken out of the different branches and put under marketing will be dealt with under the marketing vote.
I should like to ask the minister how many dairy cows there are in Canada?

I am afraid the minister is out by many millions. How many of them are under test?

Will the minister explain why the vote for dairying is so small in proportion to some of the other votes for agriculture? Last year I gave the house a few figures showing the relative importance of dairying as a branch of agriculture. I do not wish to be understood as finding any fault with the size of the votes allotted 'to the other branches, but it would seem to me that, in view of the relative importance of dairying as compared with other branches of agriculture, its vote is quite small. The value of animals and animal products from 1932 to 1936 was approximately S636.000.000; of our poultry and egg products, $327,000,000; of our dairy produce, $1,169,000,000, and of our wheat, $900,000,000. When we consider the size of the vote in comparison with the importance of these different branches of agriculture, the amount of money that is derived from them and their value to the industry itself, it seems to me that a very small amount is being expended for daily purposes. It is not necessary for me to go into percentages. I think the amount of the dairy vote is something like four per cent of the total vote for agriculture. The vote for live stock amounts to about twenty per cent. If one turns to the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, one will find nearly $2,000,000 is allocated for the administration of the Canada Grain Act alone, which has largely to do with the sale and marketing of wheat.

My argument is that if it is necessary to expend large amounts to market our wheat successfully, which has a value considerably smaller than our dairy products, the amount allowed here is too small, and I think the minister might very well explain to the committee why this vote is so small.

The vote for dairying has been increased this year by $18,000. It was increased last year. I might draw to the attention of the committee the fact that the subsidies paid for cold storage are an assistance to dairying.
And to other branches as well.

The item for live stock, including assistance to fairs and exhibitions- a considerable percentage of that is intended to be assistance to dairying. Experimental farms, including investigations concerning plant diseases-a large part of that vote is in order to encourage dairying and to make it possible for dairy farmers to have better stock and better feed for their dairy stock. The health of animals, administration of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, an expenditure of $1,817,000-a very considerable part of that is to improve the dairy herds through improving the health of the cows throughout the country. I might say that the greater part of the vote is really a vote for dairying. It can be very easily argued and shown that more of the vote is spent for dairying than for anything else.
